Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and similarly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also adds chip). However, PGS003725 comes from a clearly disease-focused, modern multi-ancestry CAD PRS study with broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/MAE/SAS) and reports strong PRS effect sizes (HR 1.75, OR 2.14 per SD), which is strong evidence of discriminative signal even without PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS000013 provides a PRS-comparable R2=0.04 (below the CAD heritability ceiling, so plausible), but its main visible AUROC (0.81) is full-model and not PRS-only, and it lacks effect-size evidence here; overall it looks more like an older, general framework-style score. Given the stronger disease-focused multi-ancestry design plus strong OR/HR evidence, PGS003725 is more likely to transfer well in external benchmarks despite missing PRS-only R2.

PGS003580 is better supported for the target depressive disorder because its endpoint is explicitly Major Depressive Disorder (lifetime) with coherent trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported alignment, and it provides substantially richer study context (training cohort UKB, training n=67,164, and a multi-ancestry evaluation distribution with validation n=42,250). Although its only reported metric is an R²=0.0254 that appears to be full-model/unspecified (not PRS-only), PGS002759 also lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² and provides less development detail (samples_training N/A, no training cohorts listed) with only a single EUR evaluation record; its OR per SD=1.26 suggests relatively weak-to-moderate PRS signal. With both candidates missing clean PRS-only metrics, the stronger endpoint specificity and broader validation context favor PGS003580.

Both candidates match the target trait well (all-cause dementia; EFO=dementia), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004281 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator. PGS005170 is better-supported structurally and for external transfer: it is an explicit multi-score integrative/ensemble PRS built from genome-wide methods (LDpred2/PRS-CS/C+T) with very large variant count (1,320,229) and multi-ancestry evaluation (including AFR/AMR/EAS as well as EUR), plus it reports a PRS-associated effect size (HR 1.25). In contrast, PGS004281 is a very sparse 110-variant single-UKB score with EUR-only development/evaluation and no effect-size evidence, making it more likely to be less robust outside its single-biobank setting despite its larger internal training/validation sizes.

PGS000823 is better supported as a transferable dementia-relevant PRS because it comes from a disease-focused Alzheimer’s/dementia cohort study context with an explicit time-to-event effect size (HR 1.36 top vs bottom tertile) and a multi-cohort AD genetics development background, whereas PGS004281 is a single-UKB (framework/method) score whose only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC (0.819) with covariates (age/sex/PCs) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its apparent performance largely non-comparable for PRS ranking. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (all-cause dementia vs incident all-cause dementia), but PGS004281 lacks PRS-isolated performance evidence and is more likely internally optimized to UKB, while PGS000823 provides at least PRS-linked risk separation evidence in an externally oriented setting.

PGS001783 is the better-supported COPD PRS on the visible fields: it has direct endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease”) and, crucially, reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / pgs_only_r2=0.038092), which is also plausible relative to the provided COPD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0388). It is developed in a broad multi-biobank/global context (many cohorts listed) with basic covariates (sex, age, PCs), reducing concerns about risk-factor packaging. In contrast, PGS004536 is explicitly a risk-factor integration metaPRS (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”), has unknown covariates, provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 (only an OR=1.49 without context), and uses a narrower single-biobank development cohort (UKB only) with an ICD-code subtype label (J44) rather than the generic COPD endpoint. Overall, PGS001783 has cleaner, more directly comparable PRS evidence and a more externally oriented development setting than PGS004536.

PGS004254 is the stronger choice on structural and endpoint grounds: it targets a direct Crohn’s disease diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Crohn’s disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,682), plus it reports a strong effect size (OR 2.18), suggesting meaningful PRS signal even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided (its AUROC=0.72 is full-model and not directly comparable). PGS001330, while it does provide clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.576; PGS-only R2 0.00621, below the heritability ceiling) and has multi-ancestry evaluation, comes from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework archetype (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse 220-variant snpnet model and a time-to-event phenotype formulation, both of which are warning signals for external transfer versus a disease-focused genome-wide score. Overall, the framework+sparsity penalties for PGS001330 outweigh its modest PRS-only metric advantage, making PGS004254 more likely to rank higher in real-world performance.

PGS004614 is the more disease-focused, endpoint-faithful diverticular disease PRS (Cell Genomics diverticular disease study; phenotyping_reported = “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very large variant coverage (1,082,282), which is structurally favored for polygenic disease prediction over sparse framework scores. PGS000997 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”), a study archetype that tends to generalize worse despite clean PRS-only metrics; its PRS-only AUROC is modest (0.591) and the time-to-event endpoint adds additional mismatch risk for a generic disease target. Although PGS004614 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.76) and includes family history (making that AUROC non-comparable as PRS-only evidence), the overall study archetype + method/variant-count signals still favor it over the UKB framework sparse model.

Both candidates align to COPD (same trait_efo; candidate_a uses ICD-10 J44 COPD code, candidate_b uses generic COPD), so endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both. Candidate_a (PGS004536) has stronger PRS-discrimination evidence via a per-SD OR=1.49 (near the ≥1.5 ‘strong’ guideline) and uses an explicit multi-score aggregation/meta-PRS approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with slightly higher variant count, which domain guidance treats as a positive structural signal. Candidate_b (PGS001788) provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.0163) that is plausible under the COPD heritability ceiling, but it comes from a known portability/framework-style ‘Global Biobank analyses…’ archetype and its full-model AUROC=0.715 is not PRS-comparable; the PRS-only R2 is modest. Given the framework penalty and weaker PRS signal magnitude, candidate_a is more likely to transfer better despite missing explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo = major depressive disorder; EUR GWAS/EVAL only) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparability is limited. PGS002759 has cleaner disclosed evaluation adjustment (age, sex, 10 PCs, technical covariates) and provides a directly interpretable PRS effect size (OR per SD = 1.26, 95% CI 1.22–1.30), whereas PGS003333 reports only a small Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 (0.022) that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric with covariates listed as 'Unknown', reducing interpretability. Validation sizes are similar (39,444 vs 34,703) and method/variant counts are near-identical, so the clearer covariate disclosure plus interpretable OR evidence makes PGS002759 better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and direct phenotyping_reported). PGS002092 is structurally stronger and more likely to transfer: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (484,484 vs 11 for PGS001254) and, crucially, is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS) rather than EUR-only, which is supportive for robustness beyond UKB-European settings. Although PGS001254 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.665; R2=0.0247), it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“813 traits”) with an extremely sparse snpnet model, a pattern associated with weaker external generalization; its metric advantage is modest and not enough to outweigh PGS002092’s stronger method/coverage and broader evaluation context despite PGS002092 lacking PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS004951 is better supported for dilated cardiomyopathy because it provides PRS-isolated performance evidence (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), whereas PGS004861 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.70/0.048) without isolating the PRS contribution, making its discrimination less comparable. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both map to dilated cardiomyopathy; PGS004951’s “Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy” is at least as specific as PGS004861’s generic label), and MTAG is not a negative signal here. Although PGS004861 has a much larger evaluation sample (n=347,585 vs n=7,761) and includes age/sex covariates, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh PGS004951’s clearer PRS-only metrics plus stronger reported effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.56).

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation context (same multi-ancestry eval distribution; selected European validation; same validation N=18,971). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes for either, the main differentiators are structural: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (484,484 variants) versus PGS001880’s sparse penalized regression score (2,443 variants). The selected partial correlation is also slightly higher for PGS002092 (0.0797 vs 0.0783), though the gap is small. Given identical endpoint and covariate context, the genome-wide model plus marginally better partial-r makes PGS002092 better-supported.

Both candidates target dilated cardiomyopathy with the same reported trait label ("Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)") and same method (PRS-CS) with EUR evaluation, so endpoint alignment is broadly comparable; candidate_b (PGS004951) is slightly more clinically explicit in phenotyping_reported ("Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy") than candidate_a (PGS004862: "Dilated cardiomyopathy"). Critically, PGS004951 provides PRS-comparable evidence (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 [0.65–0.69] and delta liability-scale R²=0.101) and a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.93 vs 1.76), with PRS-only R² remaining below the provided liability h² ceiling (~0.172), supporting plausibility. PGS004862 reports only full-model AUROC=0.71 and R²=0.05 (with age/sex covariates), which is not directly comparable as PRS-only performance and could be covariate-driven; despite its much larger validation sample (n=347,585 vs 7,761), validation size is a weak tie-breaker when PRS-only metrics are missing. Therefore PGS004951 is better-supported on comparable PRS performance and effect-size evidence.

Both candidates have clean endpoint fidelity for gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model metrics can’t be used as direct PRS comparators. However, PGS004047 provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence via effect sizes (OR per SD ~2.0 with CI) and multiple validation records with a large evaluation sample (n=90,274) and some ancestry breadth in evaluation (EUR+SAS). In contrast, PGS004768 reports only an incremental/full-model R2 (0.081) with basic covariates and no effect sizes, and has much smaller validation (n=9,462) and EUR-only evaluation. Given the richer, more directly PRS-informative performance evidence (effect sizes) and broader validation context, PGS004047 is better supported than PGS004768.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=follicular lymphoma; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Nodular lymphoma), from the same publication, with identical training (n=3,696), validation size (n=3,256), ancestry (EUR-only), and covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean comparable PRS metrics; the small full-model AUROC difference is likely noise. As a tie-break, PGS000644 shows slightly stronger overall discrimination signals (higher full-model AUROC 0.538 vs 0.532; higher per-SD OR 1.149 vs 1.133) and much larger variant count (2.21M vs 1.05M), while PGS000643’s advantage is mainly the top-1% OR (2.49 vs 1.48) with wide CIs. Overall evidence marginally favors PGS000644.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training cohort (UKB), training size (n=269,704), covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), and similar multi-ancestry evaluation distribution, so the decision rests on endpoint fidelity and PRS-only performance. PGS000997 targets a direct ICD-style endpoint aligned to the target trait ("Diverticular disease of intestine"; phenotyping_reported TTE diverticular disease of intestine), whereas PGS000996 mixes in diverticulitis in trait_efo/phenotyping ("diverticular disease, diverticulitis"), slightly diluting fidelity to the generic diverticular disease target. Empirically, PGS000997 also has materially stronger PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591 vs 0.552; PGS-only R2 0.0178 vs 0.0037) and a much larger variant set (5757 vs 368), suggesting better captured polygenic signal. Although PGS000997 uses a time-to-event phenotype (a mild warning signal), within this same study family its clearly stronger PRS-only discrimination outweighs PGS000996’s larger validation N.

PGS000644 is better supported as a transferable PRS for follicular lymphoma because it is a genome-wide lassosum score with ~2.2M variants and reports PRS-linked effect sizes (OR per SD 1.149) plus additional metrics (Nagelkerke R², Brier, top-1% OR), with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch). In contrast, PGS002304 uses only 6 genome-wide significant variants and provides no PRS-only metrics or effect sizes; its only visible discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.61 with unknown covariates and a very small validation sample (n=197), making the apparent AUC advantage hard to interpret as PRS-driven. Although PGS002304 has cleaner endpoint labeling (follicular lymphoma vs 'nodular lymphoma'), both map to the same EFO, and the much stronger methodological/structural evidence favors PGS000644.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to dupuytren contracture (same EFO; phenotyping_reported is direct disease/contracture wording in both). PGS001254 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; PGS-only R2 0.0247) but comes from the pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant model, which is a known warning pattern for weaker external transfer. PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a much denser penalized-regression score (2443 variants) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger portability/robustness evidence than PGS001254’s EUR-only evaluation. Given the framework+sparsity concerns for PGS001254 and the broader evaluation context plus richer genome coverage for PGS001880, PGS001880 is more likely to generalize despite missing directly comparable metrics.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo major depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported is MDD), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show small full-model/overall R2: 0.022 for PGS003333 vs 0.0254 for PGS003580, a negligible gap and not PRS-comparable). Given metrics can’t cleanly differentiate, structural/study-design signals dominate: PGS003333 is built with PRS-CS-auto (genome-wide shrinkage, generally stronger for highly polygenic traits) and is developed from multiple major depression GWAS sources (23andMe + PGC + UKB), whereas PGS003580 uses PRSice-2 (thresholding) and is UKB-only for training/development. Although PGS003580 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation listed, its selected validation ancestry is still European and the main advantage otherwise is variant count, which is less informative across different method families. Overall, PGS003333 looks more robustly disease-GWAS-supported and methodologically stronger for external performance.

PGS001792 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target via an explicit clinical subtype (Primary open-angle glaucoma) with matching phenotyping_reported, and it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / pgs_only_r2=0.03209) that is interpretable as PRS signal. PGS002761 is label-aligned (Glaucoma) and reports a strong OR per SD (1.68), but it lacks any PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and comes from a family-history comparison framework where the PRS evidence is less directly quantified on the record. Both use only basic covariates and EUR evaluation, but the presence of an explicit PRS-only R2 plus multi-cohort development context in PGS001792 outweighs PGS002761’s single effect-size-only support.

Both candidates target primary open-angle glaucoma, but PGS001792 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.03209, which is directly interpretable as PRS signal (and is below the glaucoma heritability ceiling, so not obviously inflated). PGS004944 provides only a full-model AUROC (0.748) plus an OR=1.74 without any PGS-only AUC/R2, and its phenotyping is explicitly self-reported, adding endpoint noise. While PGS004944 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and a disease-focused ophthalmology context, the lack of PRS-only metrics and the self-reported endpoint make it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS001792’s explicit PRS-only R2 evidence.

PGS004614 is the better-supported same-trait choice because it is a disease-focused diverticular disease study (Cell Genom; “150 risk variants…”) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very large genome-wide coverage (1,082,282 variants) and explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS000996 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits…”, snpnet) with a very small variant set (368) and weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5519; PGS R2 0.00372), which is consistent with underpowered/underperforming framework sparse scores despite clean metric reporting. Although PGS004614 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.76) and includes family history (making that AUROC non-comparable as PRS-only), the overall study archetype + method/coverage signals favor it over the framework sparse score whose PRS-only metrics are clearly low.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry distribution MAE 100%, same validation sample size n=94,651, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 with only full-model AUROC reported and covariates unknown). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially identical, the main differentiators are the available effect-size signal and the reported AUROC: PGS005271 shows stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; β 0.44 vs 0.35) and a modestly higher full-model AUROC (0.630 vs 0.605). Variant counts are effectively identical. Given the domain guidance that OR magnitude is a meaningful supportive signal when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005271 is better supported than PGS005272.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate gout). However, PGS004160 provides materially richer and more PRS-informative validation evidence: it reports effect sizes (OR per SD ~2.05) and a full-model AUROC (~0.694) across multiple performance records, and it is evaluated not only in EUR but also includes SAS in EVAL (67%/33%), supporting broader transportability. In contrast, PGS004768 reports only an incremental R2 (0.081) from a covariate model (age/sex/PCs) with no AUROC, no PRS-only metrics, and no effect sizes, making its PRS contribution harder to benchmark. Despite PGS004768 having larger training N and more variants, the lack of directly interpretable PRS performance evidence versus PGS004160’s stronger validation/effect-size support makes PGS004160 the better-supported choice.

PGS002304 has the cleanest endpoint fidelity to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” matching the target directly, whereas PGS000643 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the same EFO term, introducing avoidable phenotype ambiguity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS002304 shows higher reported AUROC (0.61 vs 0.532 for PGS000643). PGS000643 has stronger structural properties (PRS-CS, ~1.0M variants, larger validation n=3,256 and explicit basic covariates), but given the primary importance of phenotype alignment and the lack of PRS-only metrics to justify overriding that, PGS002304 is better-supported on the visible fields for follicular lymphoma.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication and release date, same MVP development cohort, same basic covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same multi-ancestry GWAS/EVAL distribution, and same validation sample size (n=31,804). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 or incremental AUC, so the full-model C-index (~0.753) is not a strong differentiator and the tiny gap (0.75368 vs 0.75325) is essentially noise. The only meaningful visible separation is slightly stronger effect-size evidence for PGS005083 (OR 1.455 vs 1.443) alongside a marginally higher full-model C-index, so PGS005083 is weakly better-supported on the available fields.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), covariates (0), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not directly comparable PRS metrics). Given this, the best differentiators are within-family empirical performance and structural signals: PGS004160 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) shows consistently stronger reported full-model discrimination and effect size than PGS004047 (LDpred2.CV): higher AUROC (0.6936 vs 0.6851), higher R² (0.0893 vs 0.0801), and slightly higher OR per SD (2.05 vs 2.00). Additionally, MultiPRS (ensemble/multi-score aggregation) is a positive structural signal versus a single-score method when other fields are matched. The advantage is modest, so confidence is Moderate.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (phenotyping_reported/trait_efo match), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same evaluation setup/ancestry distribution and validation N (31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With metrics essentially tied (full-model C-index 0.75368 vs 0.75358; OR per SD 1.455 vs 1.452 with overlapping CIs), the only slight edge is candidate_a (PGS005083) showing marginally higher C-index and OR, while candidate_b’s slightly higher variant count is not decisive across different methods. Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to the target (same trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, and have identical evaluation ancestry and validation sample size, so phenotype and transportability do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only AUROC shown is full-model and thus not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator, and the small full-model AUROC edge for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.605) is not decisive given unknown covariates. With PRS-comparable metrics absent, structural and effect-size signals dominate: PGS005272 uses PRSCS (genome-wide shrinkage) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.42) than PGS005270 (OR≈1.04) which is a sparse P+T score with 55 variants. This combination makes PGS005272 better-supported as the stronger standalone PRS for external performance.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (good match to heart failure), same EFO, same method (LDpred), same variant count, same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age/sex/20 PCs; no heavy leakage), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=31,804) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model C-index). With no PRS-comparable metrics to separate them, the only visible differentiator is slightly stronger reported performance/effect size for PGS005077 (full-model C-index 0.7536 vs 0.7532; OR per SD 1.452 vs 1.443). The differences are tiny, so confidence is low, but PGS005077 has the marginal edge.

PGS004944 is better supported for the target trait glaucoma because its endpoint is a clinically specific and coherent match to glaucoma (primary open-angle glaucoma; EFO open-angle glaucoma) and it shows broader transportability evidence with multi-ancestry GWAS input and multi-ancestry validation listed (selected_validation_ancestry spans African, Hispanic/LatAm, East/South Asian, European) plus a very large evaluation sample (n=407,667). Although its only AUROC is a full-model AUROC (0.748) and thus not PRS-comparable, it at least provides discrimination context alongside a strong per-SD OR (1.74). In contrast, PGS002761 has a broader/less specific phenotype label ("Glaucoma"), is EUR-only in both GWAS and evaluation, has much smaller validation (n=39,444), and provides only an OR (1.68) with no AUC/R2 context at all. With neither candidate reporting PRS-only AUC/R2, the combination of stronger effect size and substantially broader validation/ancestry support favors PGS004944.

PGS001320 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R2=0.06493) with basic covariates and a clear hypertension endpoint, giving interpretable evidence of standalone PRS signal (and the R2 is plausibly below the hypertension heritability ceiling). In contrast, PGS004234 is from a disease-focused multi-ethnic hypertension study and has broader evaluation ancestries, but it reports only a full-model AUROC (0.763) with a heavier covariate set (including BMI and smoking) and no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes, making its apparent performance largely non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven. Given the benchmark goal of PRS transfer/performance, the cleaner PRS-only metric evidence in PGS001320 outweighs PGS004234’s study framing and ancestry breadth.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity and study context (same reported trait/phenotyping: Hodgkin's disease; same EFO mapping; same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL; same cohorts, covariates, training n=736 and validation n=775; no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal). Given that, PGS000639 has consistently stronger available performance/effect evidence than PGS000638: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). With covariates identical and no leakage signals, these modest but consistent advantages make PGS000639 better-supported.

Both candidates target the same endpoint with identical phenotype fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma), identical ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI), same training size (n=736), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so we must rely on the available full-model/effect-size evidence. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000637: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), higher per-SD OR (1.476 vs 1.3), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.67). Given the same study context and covariate set, these stronger empirical metrics outweigh PGS000637’s more complex method/huge variant count (PRS-CS, 1,047,511 variants), making PGS000639 the better-supported choice here.

PGS004236 is from a hypertension-focused, multi-ethnic study (Nat Commun) with multi-cohort development (BioMe, MVP, UKB) and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1 per SD), which is meaningful PRS-discrimination evidence even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided and the reported AUROC (0.764) is full-model with additional covariates (including BMI/smoking). In contrast, PGS001320 comes from a pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically less transferable; despite clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649) and larger training/validation, its framework archetype and single-biobank development make it less likely to rank best in external benchmarks than the disease-focused multi-cohort score.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported trait/phenotyping (M16 coxarthrosis), same EFO (hip osteoarthritis), same publication/date, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (174,489), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count (1,059,939), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR reported). With metrics otherwise unavailable, the only differentiator is the reported effect size: PGS004478 has a higher OR per SD (1.296) than PGS004548 (1.216), suggesting stronger PRS signal. Method differences (LDpred2 vs RFDiseasemetaPRS) are not supported by any additional comparable performance evidence here, so the higher OR breaks the tie in favor of PGS004478.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: lymphocytic thyroiditis; trait_efo: Hashimoto's thyroiditis), come from the same publication, have the same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a reliable cross-model PRS metric). With endpoint and validation context essentially tied, structural/effect-size evidence breaks the tie: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.55, β≈0.44), consistent with meaningful PRS signal, whereas PGS005270 is a very sparse P+T score (55 variants) with a near-null effect size (OR≈1.04, β≈0.04). The slightly higher full-model AUROC for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.630) is small and likely noise given unknown covariates and lack of PRS-only metrics, so PGS005271 is better-supported as the stronger standalone PRS.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target via trait_efo = osteoarthritis, hip and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (so metrics can’t separate them). PGS002763 has slightly better endpoint fidelity/clarity for the generic target (“Hip osteoarthritis” in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported) and discloses a clean, basic covariate set (age, sex, PCs, technical), reducing concern about packaged/augmented prediction. PGS004478 uses an ICD-style label (M16 coxarthrosis) which is still aligned, but has unknown covariates and comes from a ‘risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration’ framing that raises mild packaging/augmentation concern without providing PRS-only metrics to verify standalone performance. Effect-size evidence is also a bit stronger for PGS002763 (OR 1.38 with CI) vs PGS004478 (OR ~1.30 without CI).

Both candidates are from the same Nat Commun paper, target the same trait (hypertension) with the same phenotyping_reported (prevalent hypertension), use the same covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), and have essentially identical full-model AUROC (0.764 for PGS004236 vs 0.763 for PGS004234) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so metrics don’t meaningfully differentiate. PGS004236 has stronger supportive evidence via a reported PRS effect size (OR=2.1, 95% CI 1.99–2.21) that PGS004234 lacks, and it reflects a broader development/training context (BioMe+MVP+UKB vs BioMe+UKB) with a higher variant count (398,805 vs 234,228), which is a modest structural advantage given otherwise near-clone design.

Both candidates map cleanly to hip osteoarthritis (same trait_efo), but PGS002763 has higher endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis”) whereas PGS004548 is an ICD-style label (“M16 Coxarthrosis”), which is close but less directly aligned to the target wording. Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect size is the main performance signal: PGS002763 shows a materially stronger OR per SD (1.38, CI 1.31–1.46) than PGS004548 (OR 1.216). PGS002763 also has disclosed basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), while PGS004548 has covariates unknown and comes from a risk-factor integration study archetype, which is a mild comparability concern. Although PGS004548 has larger validation N and a stated training N, those are weak tie-breakers versus the stronger effect-size evidence and cleaner phenotype/covariate transparency in PGS002763.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same cohorts, covariates, training n=736 and validation n=775) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family comparator. Within this identical setting, PGS000638 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000637: higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013), with slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.377 vs 1.30). Although PGS000637 uses a genome-wide PRS-CS model with many variants, the observed validation metrics in this same publication family favor PGS000638, making it the better-supported choice here.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet paper with identical endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; trait_efo matches), identical basic covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same development cohorts, and same validation sample size (n=343,182). Neither reports PRS-only AUROC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal. Within this otherwise matched setting, PGS004911 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5), and it is explicitly the MTAG-enhanced variant, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base version when endpoints are the same.

PGS005218 is better supported overall: it comes from a clearly disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large genome-wide coverage (1,110,091 variants), and has much larger evaluation support (n=441,692 EUR). In contrast, PGS004935 is from a portability/framework-style paper, is a sparse SnpNet score with only 6,127 variants and single-cohort development (UKB), with small evaluation (n=8,417). Although PGS005218 reports a higher full-model AUROC (0.859 vs 0.7), its covariates include near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) making that AUROC non-comparable to PRS-only performance; however PGS004935 also lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and provides only an OR=1.5 effect size, so the decision falls back to endpoint/study archetype and structural signals, which favor PGS005218.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to overall JIA, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a broad JIA target). Both are from the same disease-focused publication, same method (SparSNP), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, and similarly basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). Although PGS000325 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.738) and larger validation N, full-model AUROC is discounted as a cross-model PRS metric and the subtype restriction reduces fidelity for the broad target; PGS000114 also has slightly stronger OR per SD (2.085 vs 1.93) and more variants (26 vs 21).

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to the broad JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA), which is a narrower endpoint and therefore less faithful for a generic JIA target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have the same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, so study archetype and covariate leakage do not differentiate them. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the small full-model AUROC difference (0.76 vs 0.738) is not decisive; instead, PGS000114 also shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) and has a larger variant set (26 vs 12), supporting stronger standalone PRS signal while retaining the correct broad endpoint.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and validation design/ancestry mix (same EVAL distribution; n=19,883; selected European record). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes for either, the main differentiators are the PRS-comparable metric available (partial-r) and structural properties. PGS002031 has slightly higher partial correlation (0.1355 vs 0.1307) and is a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with substantially more variants (6,713 vs 654), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal in this framework setting. PGS001823 is slightly weaker on partial-r and is much sparser, offering less evidence it will transfer better.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to hypothyroidism) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and comparability signals plus effect sizes. PGS002766 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (1,092,122 variants) and explicitly reports only basic demographic/PC/technical covariates, which is a clean, comparable evaluation setup. PGS004935 is a sparse SnpNet score (6,127 variants) from a portability-style paper and its only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.70 (not PRS-comparable) with covariates listed as unknown, making its apparent performance harder to interpret. Effect sizes are similar (OR 1.47 for PGS002766 vs 1.50 for PGS004935), so the method/variant-coverage and cleaner covariate disclosure favor PGS002766 despite PGS004935’s larger stated training N.

Both candidates align well to the target endpoint (phenotyping_reported and trait_efo are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a reliable differentiator—especially since PGS000739’s AUROC is from a covariate-heavy model including multiple clinical risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making its discrimination less attributable to the PRS. PGS004911 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far greater variant coverage (374,114 vs 27) and reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (OR per SD 1.33; HR 2.34; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, which is more comparable and less clinically packaged. Given similar disease-focused cohort context, the cleaner covariate design plus genome-wide shrinkage structure makes PGS004911 more likely to transfer as a standalone PRS than the sparse, clinically augmented PGS000739.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS000739’s higher full-model AUROC (0.821 vs 0.73) is heavily discounted because it is paired with substantial clinical covariates (obesity, HTN, AF, CAD and rare-variant carrier status), which likely inflate discrimination beyond the PRS contribution. In contrast, PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, sex, PCs), making its reported effects more indicative of the PRS itself; it also shows strong PRS-associated effect sizes (HR 1.97; OR high vs median tertile 5.5) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with far more variants (374,190 vs 27), which is structurally more appropriate for capturing polygenic signal than a GWAS-hits-only score. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for external transfer, while PGS000739 looks more like a clinically packaged risk model.

Both candidates are near-clones: same Graves’ disease endpoint (a strong match to hyperthyroidism), same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either. With no PRS-comparable metrics, the only differentiators are small full-model AUROC and effect sizes; PGS005265 is slightly stronger on both (full-model AUROC 0.6652 vs 0.6637; OR per SD 1.625 vs 1.543), while PGS005266 has no compensating advantage beyond a trivially different cohort list. Given the tiny metric gaps and lack of PRS-only reporting, confidence is low but PGS005265 is marginally better-supported.

PGS005266 is a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank score for Graves’ disease (a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism per the provided domain guidance) with very strong genome-wide coverage (1,085,170 variants; PRSCS) and supportive PRS effect-size evidence (OR≈1.54 per SD). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC≈0.664 with unknown covariates), its study archetype and method/variant structure are more consistent with robust external transfer than PGS001043. PGS001043 has exact label alignment to hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis and clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6323; R2=0.0216, below the h2 ceiling), but it comes from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) with only 69 variants—an archetype explicitly noted to generalize poorly versus disease-focused multi-cohort models. Net: PGS005266’s endpoint-as-dominant-subtype plus stronger disease-focused multi-biobank design and genome-wide shrinkage outweigh PGS001043’s cleaner but modest PRS-only metrics from a framework sparse model.

PGS004908 is better supported as a standalone kidney-cancer PRS: it is from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) with a much larger GWAS-hit set (107 variants vs 19 for PGS000076) and shows a substantially stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5 vs HR per SD 1.16), which is a key proxy for PRS discriminative power when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and only report similar full-model AUROC (~0.74 vs ~0.72) with broadly similar epidemiologic covariates, so the small AUROC difference is not decisive; the stronger effect size and richer disease-specific discovery evidence favor PGS004908 over the older cross-cancer evaluation score PGS000076 (despite PGS000076’s slightly larger validation N and incident endpoint wording).

PGS004562 is the better match to the target trait “kidney failure” on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is exactly kidney failure and phenotyping_reported is ICD code N18 chronic renal failure, which is closer to failure than candidate_b’s CKD stage ≥3 definition (eGFR <45) and trait_efo of chronic kidney disease. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and effect-size evidence; PGS004562 uses an explicit meta/ensemble-style approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with larger genome-wide variant coverage (~1.06M vs 0.47M) and has a reasonable OR per SD (1.40). PGS002237 has a slightly higher OR (1.47) and broader multi-ancestry evaluation, but its only AUROC shown (0.78) is a full-model metric with a heavy covariate set (including hypertension, diabetes, BMI, medication use), making it less informative about standalone PRS quality and more susceptible to covariate-driven inflation. Overall, the tighter kidney-failure endpoint alignment plus stronger structural signals favor PGS004562.

Both candidates are essentially the same 19-variant RCC/kidney cancer PRS evaluated in EUR with the same incident endpoint, identical covariates, identical validation sample size (n=391,610), and nearly identical full-model discrimination/effect size (AUROC 0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724; HR per SD 1.16 for PGS000076 vs 1.15 for PGS000787). However, PGS000787 explicitly states it uses the same variants as PGS000076 but with inverse weights, which is a strong structural red flag (likely degrading the PRS signal rather than improving it) without any compensating PRS-only metric advantage (both lack PGS-only AUC/R2). The extra R²=0.366 reported for PGS000787 appears to be a full-model/other metric and is not PRS-comparable, and is also implausibly high relative to the kidney cancer heritability ceiling context, so it should not drive selection. Therefore the original, non-inverted score PGS000076 is better-supported.

Both candidates align well to the target (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS000053 is better supported by a cleaner, disease-focused multi-cohort development/validation context (many AD cohorts listed; covariates explicitly limited to age and sex) and it provides a PRS-relevant effect size (OR=1.29 per SD), giving at least some direct evidence of discriminative signal. PGS000334 reports only a generic R²=0.191 that appears to be full-model/unspecified (not PRS-only) with unknown covariates, making the metric hard to interpret and potentially inflated; its training context is narrower (IGAP, UKB) and GWAS ancestry includes an NR component. Validation sizes are similar and not decisive.

PGS004908 is better supported as a standalone kidney-cancer PRS: it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 1.43–1.58), whereas PGS000787 is a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework score built from only 19 variants with a weaker PRS signal (HR 1.15, 1.07–1.24). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.74 vs 0.722) is not decisive and is further confounded by covariate-heavy models in both; in that setting, the stronger disease-focused study archetype plus materially stronger effect size and larger variant set favor PGS004908 over the more packaged, cross-cancer model PGS000787.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD). However, PGS000054 has stronger PRS-relevant empirical support on the visible fields: it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), which is a meaningful PRS discrimination signal when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. PGS000334 provides only an R²=0.191 that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric (not labeled PRS-only) with unknown covariates, making it non-comparable and potentially inflated; it also conflicts with the low heritability ceiling context, further reducing trust. Transportability is mixed (PGS000054 evaluated in AMR/Hispanic; PGS000334 evaluated in EUR), but this does not outweigh the stronger, cleaner PRS-specific effect-size evidence and clearer basic covariates (age, sex) for PGS000054 versus unknown covariates for PGS000334.

PGS005218 is better supported as a hypothyroidism PRS because it comes from a disease-focused GWAS/prediction study with explicit large-scale multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and a very large evaluation sample (n=441,692), whereas PGS002766 is from a cross-disease comparison paper with sparse model-specific metadata (training sample listed as N/A) and only a single validation record (n=39,444). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics can’t cleanly differentiate; however, PGS005218’s only reported AUROC is a full-model value (0.859) that is heavily covariate-inflated by thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), so it is discounted rather than treated as PRS evidence. Even with that caveat, PGS005218’s endpoint is clearly specified as incident hypothyroidism and its overall study/evidence package is stronger than PGS002766, whose main quantitative support is an OR per SD of 1.47 (moderate) without broader validation context.

PGS005265 is better-supported for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves' disease) is a clinically dominant and directly relevant subtype of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort/multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation (validation n=94,651; eval MAE; selected validation ancestries include African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, and European). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.63), which is meaningful PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (0.665) and PRS-only AUC/R2 are missing. In contrast, PGS001043 has an exact label match and clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6323; R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB '813 traits' sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants) which is penalized for weaker external transfer reliability and is trained only in EUR with selected validation shown as European despite mixed eval ancestries. Overall, the disease-focused multi-biobank design plus strong OR makes PGS005265 more likely to generalize for hyperthyroidism than the UKB framework sparse score.

PGS002237 is better supported on visible evidence despite being mapped to chronic kidney disease rather than the exact kidney failure EFO: its phenotyping is a clear clinical severity endpoint (CKD stage ≥3; eGFR<45) and it reports substantially stronger PRS signal (OR=1.47 with CI) plus an AUROC=0.78 (not PRS-only, but at least quantified with CI). It also shows broader evaluation across multiple ancestries, suggesting more transportability evidence than PGS004492. In contrast, PGS004492 has closer endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=kidney failure; ICD N18 chronic renal failure) and a stronger method/variant-count profile (LDpred2; ~1.06M variants), but it provides very thin performance support (single record, no AUC/R2, only a modest OR≈1.17 without CI) and unknown covariates, making its real PRS discriminative strength less evidenced than PGS002237.

PGS000754 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Systemic lupus erythematosus,” which is the best-matched heritability reference in the provided domain knowledge, whereas PGS002082 uses a broader/less specific endpoint (“Lupus (localized and systemic)”) from a UKB portability framework paper. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002082’s partial correlation (partial-r=0.0212) is weak and not clearly more informative than PGS000754’s reported AUROC=0.65 (not PRS-only and covariates unknown). Given the framework-penalty signal for the UKB portability archetype and the stronger disease-focused publication context for SLE in PGS000754, PGS000754 is better-supported overall despite less complete training metadata.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same ICD-10 N18 chronic renal failure; trait_efo kidney failure), study context (same Commun Biol paper), variant count (1,059,939), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2.
