Although PGS004562 uses an aggregation-style method name (RFDiseasemetaPRS) versus LDpred2 for PGS004492, the decision is primarily driven by the stronger observed OR in PGS004562 given the lack of comparable AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait/EFO, same publication, same method (genome-wide significant variants) and same variant count (21), same phenotyping_reported (familial late-onset LOAD) and covariates (age, sex), and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics largely absent, the main differentiator is the reported PRS effect size: PGS000054 shows a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR 1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is stronger evidence of discriminative signal. PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-only evaluation ancestry, but validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger effect size signal in PGS000054.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as PRS performance). Given that, structural/model-quality signals dominate: PGS004860 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with ~1.14M variants, which is generally better suited to capturing polygenic signal than PGS000078’s genome-wide-significant-only 109-variant score. While PGS000078 has much larger validation n and multi-cohort development listed, its reported performance is heavily covariate-packaged (includes family history, detailed smoking variables/interactions, and PM2.5), making its high full-model AUROC less informative about PRS strength; PGS004860’s covariates are lighter (age/sex/BMI/smoking/PCs). Overall, PGS004860 is more likely to yield stronger standalone PRS transfer for lung cancer.

Both candidates are essentially the same endpoint (incident lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma), same ancestry context (EUR GWAS/EVAL), same variant count (109), same covariate-heavy evaluation model (includes family history, smoking variables/interactions, PM2.5), and they report the same full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, which is a strong negative structural signal versus the original disease score, and its additional reported R²=0.799 appears to be a full-model/packaged metric (not PRS-only) and is implausibly high relative to the provided lung-cancer heritability ceiling, so it should not be treated as better PRS evidence. With no PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the original published score (PGS000078) is better-supported than an inverted-weight derivative (PGS000789).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS000789 is from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration paper and its reported discrimination is heavily packaged with multiple non-genetic predictors including family history, detailed smoking variables with interactions, and PM2.5—making its high full-model AUROC/C-index largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS004860, while still adjusted for standard epidemiologic covariates (age/sex/BMI/smoking + PCs), is less clinically packaged and is a genome-wide LDpred2 score (1.14M variants), which is a stronger structural signal for capturing polygenic architecture than a 109-variant reweighted hits score. Given cleaner covariate packaging and stronger genome-wide construction, PGS004860 is more likely to transfer as a PRS in external benchmarking despite its smaller validation sample.

Both candidates align to the target trait (age-related macular degeneration) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not reliable for cross-model PRS ranking. Given that, PGS004952 has the cleaner ancestry compatibility (GWAS EUR and EVAL EUR) and a more endpoint-specific phenotyping label (“Late age-related macular degeneration (Clinical Classification)”), whereas PGS004607 is trained on AFR-only GWAS but evaluated in EUR, introducing a clear transportability mismatch for the selected European validation. Although PGS004607 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with many variants and has a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.48 vs 1.41), the cross-ancestry training/evaluation mismatch and lack of PRS-only metrics make it less reliably supported on the visible fields than the EUR-consistent PGS004952.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target via trait_efo (osteoarthritis, knee) and have EUR-only development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to endpoint fidelity + structural/study-design signals. PGS002767 has the cleanest direct label/phenotyping (“Knee osteoarthritis”) and disclosed basic covariates, but it comes from a cross-disease comparison paper with no training cohort/sample details and only moderate OR evidence (OR=1.35). PGS004549 uses an ICD-style knee OA endpoint (“M17 Gonarthrosis”) that is still a direct knee osteoarthritis diagnosis, has explicit development in UKB with a large stated training sample (n=174,489), slightly stronger OR (1.3667), and a method suggesting multi-score/meta-PRS integration (RFDiseasemetaPRS), which is a positive structural signal versus a single PRS-CS score when metrics are otherwise missing. Covariates are unknown for PGS004549, lowering confidence, but there is no explicit leakage/clinical risk-calculator packaging shown. Overall, PGS004549 has the stronger development/structural evidence while maintaining acceptable endpoint alignment.

PGS000754 has substantially better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: it is explicitly for systemic lupus erythematosus across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001870 uses a broader, less specific phenotype (“Lupus (localized and systemic)”) from a UKB portability framework paper. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance is hard to compare; PGS000754’s only visible metric is a full-model AUROC=0.65 (not PRS-comparable), while PGS001870 reports only a small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0184), which is weak evidence of PRS discrimination. Structurally, PGS000754 is a genome-wide shrinkage-style score with very large variant count (293,684) versus PGS001870’s very sparse 87-variant penalized regression score, and the latter’s framework/portability archetype is a known negative signal when a disease-focused alternative exists. Overall, PGS000754 is more likely to transfer as a lupus PRS despite missing PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are closely matched on study archetype (same Ann Rheum Dis paper), method (SparSNP), ancestry (DEV/EVAL EUR-only), covariates (sex + PCs 1–10), and similar training/validation sizes, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). With endpoint fidelity both are JIA subtypes rather than generic JIA, so performance/effect-size evidence becomes the main differentiator: PGS000325 shows stronger reported discrimination and PRS signal (full-model AUROC 0.80 [0.77–0.84] and OR 1.93 [1.75–2.13]) than PGS000326 (AUROC 0.76 [0.72–0.80], OR 1.51 [1.35–1.68]). Variant count is also higher for PGS000325 (21 vs 12), supporting slightly better capture of polygenic signal within the same method family.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (melanoma), identical endpoint fidelity ("Incident invasive melanoma"), same basic covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not clean PRS-comparable). With no PRS-only metrics to separate them, the small full-model differences are essentially noise; the only meaningful structural difference is that PGS002247 includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50) and is marginally higher on the reported full-model AUROC/R² (0.691/0.072 vs 0.688/0.070).

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are structural: PGS002082 uses genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2) with far more variants (361,553) and shows a slightly higher PRS-comparable partial correlation (0.0212 vs 0.0184 for PGS001870). Given identical context otherwise, the higher-signal method/coverage and marginally better partial-r support PGS002082 over the much sparser penalized-regression score.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (Age-related macular degeneration; matching trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported) and use similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10) with the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=163,011), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this near-clone setup, PGS004606 has consistently stronger visible performance signals in the selected European validation: higher full-model AUROC (0.71 vs 0.65) and a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.76 vs 1.48). Additionally, its GWAS ancestry matches the evaluation ancestry (EUR→EUR), whereas PGS004607 is trained on AFR GWAS but evaluated in EUR, a transportability mismatch that plausibly contributes to weaker EUR performance here.

PGS000648 is better aligned to a specific, clinically coherent endpoint within the target umbrella (chronic lymphocytic leukemia; phenotyping_reported: “Lymphoid leukemia, chronic”), whereas PGS000077 targets the broader “Lymphocytic leukemia” with an incident-only time-to-event framing (“Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic “lymphoid leukemia” target. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.719 for PGS000077 vs 0.696 for PGS000648) are not decisive; however PGS000648 supplies stronger PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 2.124 and top-1% OR 12.9) than PGS000077’s HR 1.45. Covariates are similarly light in both (age/sex/PCs/batch/array), so comparability is acceptable. Overall, the more endpoint-specific CLL model with stronger genetic effect-size signals (PGS000648) is more likely to transfer well than the cross-cancer incident-hazard model with weaker per-SD effect size (PGS000077).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported=Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia), use the same basic covariates, have identical variant count (75) and identical EUR-only evaluation (n=391,338), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). PGS000788 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000077 with inverse weights, which is a structural red flag rather than an evidence-backed improvement, and it is embedded in a broader “integrating PRS with modifiable risk factors” pan-cancer framing where the reported full-model metrics are not PRS-comparable. Given near-identical endpoint/validation context and lack of PRS-only metrics, the original disease score PGS000077 is better-supported and less likely to be a non-standard/incorrectly oriented reweighting than PGS000788.

Both candidates are from the same publication, target the same trait (melanoma; EFO melanoma), use the same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), and use the same basic covariates (age, sex) with EUR-only GWAS/EVAL—so endpoint fidelity and covariate comparability are essentially tied. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must treat the reported AUROC/R² as full-model and only weakly informative. Within this like-for-like setting, PGS002247 shows consistently better reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.691 vs 0.662; R² 0.072 vs 0.051) and also has a larger variant set (68 vs 45), which is a supportive structural signal. PGS002253’s much larger validation sample size is only a weak tie-breaker and does not outweigh the stronger (though still full-model) performance and higher variant count of PGS002247.

PGS000648 is the better-supported match to the target trait (lymphoid leukemia) because its endpoint is explicitly chronic lymphocytic leukemia (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both CLL), which is a clear lymphoid leukemia subtype, and it provides PRS-discriminative evidence via effect sizes (OR per SD 2.124; top 1% vs rest OR 12.9). In contrast, PGS000788 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration paper and reports only full-model discrimination (AUROC/C-index/R²) without PRS-only metrics; its very large validation sample and higher full-model AUROC (0.738 vs 0.696) are not comparable PRS evidence and may be covariate-driven. Both use only basic covariates and EUR evaluation, but PGS000648 has cleaner disease-specific PRS evidence, whereas PGS000788 is a reweighted 75-variant framework-style reuse with weaker standalone PRS support on the visible fields.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo melanoma; phenotyping_reported incident invasive melanoma), share the same publication context, and use similarly clean covariates (age, sex) with EUR-only GWAS/EVAL; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers. Given that, PGS002246 has modestly stronger reported discrimination in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.688 vs 0.662; R² 0.07 vs 0.051) and slightly more variants (50 vs 45), while PGS002253’s much larger validation_sample_size is a weak signal and does not outweigh the consistent (though non-PRS-only) performance edge for PGS002246.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma; EUR-only evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as standalone PRS performance. PGS000653 has a clearer, more interpretable evidence package: it reports additional PRS-relevant metrics/effect sizes (Nagelkerke R²=0.0145, OR per SD=1.327 with CI) and discloses basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), plus a defined training cohort (UKB) and training N=3,377. PGS002306 lacks training details, has unknown covariates, and provides only a full-model AUROC (0.69) on a small validation (n=290), which could be covariate-driven and is not a valid substitute for PRS-only performance. Therefore PGS000653 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same development cohort (MVP), identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and study context effectively tied, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size edges: PGS005039 has a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.78484 vs 0.78385) and a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.578 vs 1.554) than PGS005045. These differences are modest, so confidence is low, but they favor PGS005039.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple myeloma (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), use the same method (genome-wide significant variants) with the same variant count (23), and are EUR-only in GWAS and evaluation, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record—so the full-model AUROC difference (0.69 in PGS002306 vs 0.644 in PGS002281) is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator. PGS002281 has clearer, non-problematic covariate disclosure (age, sex, geographic region) and provides an additional PRS-relevant effect-size style metric (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 [2.34–4.33]), whereas PGS002306 lists covariates as unknown and provides no supporting effect-size metrics. Given the near-clone structure and lack of PRS-only metrics, the better-supported and more interpretable evidence package favors PGS002281.

Both candidates are near-clones: same myocardial infarction PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same method (LDpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With design essentially indistinguishable, the only differentiator is slightly stronger reported performance/effect size for PGS005039 (full-model C-index 0.7848 vs 0.7834; OR per SD 1.578 vs 1.541), so PGS005039 is marginally better-supported, though the evidence gap is very small.

PGS002767 has the cleanest endpoint fidelity to the target: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Knee osteoarthritis,” matching the target directly, whereas PGS004479 is an ICD-style label (“M17 Gonarthrosis”) that is still aligned via trait_efo but is a slightly less direct presentation. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and comparability signals: both are genome-wide shrinkage methods with ~1.05M variants and EUR-only evaluation, and their per-SD ORs are very similar (1.35 for PGS002767 vs ~1.323 for PGS004479). PGS002767 also discloses basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), avoiding ambiguity, while PGS004479 has covariates listed as unknown and comes from a “risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration” framing that can indicate packaging complexity even though no explicit leakage covariates are shown. Overall differences are small, hence low confidence, but the more direct phenotype labeling and clearer covariate context favor PGS002767.

PGS002038 and PGS000809 both have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). However, PGS002038 is a genome-wide LDpred2 score with 129,077 variants and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is stronger structural and transportability evidence than PGS000809’s very sparse 127-variant clumped score evaluated only in EUR. PGS000809 reports AUROC=0.765, but it is a full-model metric (no PGS-only AUC/R2), so it is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage; its R2=0.069 is also not explicitly PRS-only. PGS002038 at least provides a PRS-comparable partial correlation (partial-r=0.0396) and avoids relying on a potentially covariate-driven full-model AUROC. Overall, the method/variant coverage and broader evaluation context favor PGS002038 despite both lacking clean PGS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis). However, PGS002726 comes from a disease-focused MS susceptibility study (IMSGC-based) and provides stronger disease-relevant performance evidence via a large effect size (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0) plus an AUROC=0.80 that is explicitly a full-model metric (so not PRS-comparable, but still supportive within a disease-focused context). In contrast, PGS002038 is from a UKB portability framework paper (pan-trait portability archetype), which domain guidance penalizes versus disease-focused models unless it has clearly superior PRS-comparable metrics; here it reports only a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.0396) and no PRS-only AUC/R2. Although PGS002038 has broader evaluation ancestries and larger validation N, those are weak tie-breakers and do not outweigh the framework-study penalty and weaker performance signal.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; identical phenotyping_reported typo; same cohorts, ancestry_distribution, and validation_sample_size), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. Given this near-clone setting, PGS005262 is better supported by stronger available PRS signal proxies: materially larger effect size (OR 1.41, β 0.34 vs OR 1.05, β 0.047 for PGS005261) and a structurally stronger genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (PRSCS with 1,085,173 variants vs P+T with 110), alongside a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.593 vs 0.585).

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable. Still, PGS002281 comes from a disease-focused publication specifically on multiple myeloma risk prediction and shows stronger validation evidence on the visible metrics (full-model AUROC 0.644 with OR highest vs lowest quintile 3.18) than PGS000653 (full-model AUROC 0.577; OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1; per-SD OR 1.327 = only moderate). PGS000653 is from a broader repository/framework-style paper (Cancer PRSweb) and its weaker effect-size/uncertain tail OR makes it less supported here. Covariates are basic in both, and variant counts are similar (23 vs 22), so the performance/evidence package favors PGS002281.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; EFO Nasal Cavity Polyp), ancestry (DEV/EVAL EUR only), cohorts (UKB), training (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR per SD). With metrics otherwise absent, the main differentiator is the reported effect size: PGS004535 shows a stronger OR (1.60) than PGS004465 (1.35), which is supportive of better PRS discrimination. Although PGS004465 uses LDpred2 (a strong single-score shrinkage method), PGS004535’s RFDiseasemetaPRS suggests multi-score aggregation and is paired with materially stronger OR evidence within the same publication family, so PGS004535 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical endpoint fields (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Tobacco use disorder; trait_efo: nicotine dependence), identical training cohort and size (UKB, n=391,124), similar multi-ancestry evaluation context, identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and the same validation sample size (n=19,400), so the decision rests on comparable PRS signal and structural properties. PGS002037 shows stronger reported PRS signal in the selected record via higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (847,691 vs 13,838), which is generally favorable for polygenic traits when other fields are matched. PGS001830’s sparse penalized regression with much fewer variants and weaker partial-r provides less support here.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical) and come from the same study with the same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS metric). Given that, structural and effect-size evidence dominate: PGS005263 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1,085,170 variants and shows a materially stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.36, β≈0.309) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants and weak effect (OR≈1.05, β≈0.047). The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.588 vs 0.585) is essentially noise, so the stronger method/coverage and effect-size support make PGS005263 the better-supported choice.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.80 for PGS002726 vs 0.765 for PGS000809) are not cleanly comparable PRS metrics. Given that, structural/study signals dominate: PGS002726 is a disease-focused IMSGC-based score with vastly larger genome-wide coverage (476,399 variants) and a very strong risk stratification signal (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0), whereas PGS000809 is a much sparser clumped score (127 variants) whose reported R8=0.069 is likely full-model/less directly PRS-comparable and whose effect size evidence is less interpretable here (beta only). Despite PGS000809 having a larger validation sample (8,370 vs 938) and explicit basic covariates, the overall evidence package more strongly supports PGS002726 as the higher-performing transferable MS PRS.

PGS005235 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: its phenotyping_reported is an explicit obesity diagnosis ("Obesity (phecode: 278.1)") and trait_efo is obesity, whereas PGS002033 is a broader administrative/nutrition bundle ("Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation") that is less specific to obesity as a disease endpoint. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, but PGS005235 provides a strong per-SD effect size signal (OR≈1.97), while PGS002033 only shows a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079). Although PGS002033 has multi-ancestry evaluation and more variants, it comes from a UKB portability framework paper and lacks strong PRS discrimination evidence; overall the diagnosis-anchored phenotype plus strong OR makes PGS005235 the better-supported obesity PRS here.

PGS002033 is favored because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (846,292), which is structurally better aligned with a highly polygenic trait like obesity than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001298 (9,227 variants) from the known pan-trait “813 traits” framework. While PGS001298 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS-only AUROC=0.5757; R2=0.0115, below the heritability ceiling), its endpoint is explicitly time-to-event (“TTE obesity”), which is a weaker match to generic obesity than PGS002033’s broader obesity/overweight phenotype, and its framework archetype is a portability risk. Both are UKB-trained EUR with multi-ancestry evaluation, but PGS002033’s evaluation spans more ancestry groups and its partial-r evidence (0.0789) provides at least some PRS signal despite lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same (typo-identical) phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With endpoint fidelity and study context indistinguishable, the best available differentiators are the within-family effect size and the (small) full-model AUROC: PGS005262 has higher OR per SD (1.408 vs 1.362) and slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876). These consistent, albeit modest, advantages make PGS005262 the better-supported pick.

PGS001274 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.57595; PGS-only R2=0.00945) with basic covariates and a clearly specified osteoporosis endpoint (time-to-event osteoporosis without pathological fracture), plus explicit training cohort (UKB) and training N. In contrast, PGS002768 has a cleaner generic phenotype label but provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 at all (only an OR=1.31) and has ambiguous trait mapping (trait_efo includes heel bone mineral density) with missing training/development cohort and training sample size, leaving weaker visible support for expected standalone PRS performance despite its genome-wide method/variant count.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and release date, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions, same validation size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size edges: PGS005045 shows a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.78385 vs 0.78336) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.554 vs 1.541) than PGS005035. These differences are modest and full-model metrics are not PRS-comparable, so confidence is low, but the available evidence marginally favors PGS005045.

PGS005235 is better supported structurally and by study archetype for obesity risk: it is a genome-wide shrinkage score (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (709,828) and is developed from multi-cohort obesity/adiposity GWAS sources (EGG, GIANT, UKB) with a direct obesity phecode endpoint (278.1), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.97). In contrast, PGS001298 comes from a known pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“across 813 traits”) using an L1/sparse approach (snpnet) with far fewer variants (9,227) and a time-to-event obesity phenotype, which domain guidance flags as a weaker endpoint/study-design combination for external transfer despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (AUROC≈0.576; R2≈0.011). PGS005235 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2, lowering confidence, but its endpoint anchoring and disease-focused multi-cohort architecture make it more likely to generalize than the UKB framework sparse TTE score.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper, with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and the same multi-ancestry evaluation mix with selected European validation (n=24,905), so study-design/transportability signals do not differentiate them. The main difference is endpoint fidelity: PGS001273 targets generic "Osteoporosis" with phenotyping_reported="Osteoporosis", which matches the target trait directly, whereas PGS001274 is a narrower time-to-event endpoint "osteoporosis without pathological fracture" (TTE), a mild mismatch for a generic osteoporosis target. Although PGS001274 has slightly better PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.57595 vs 0.5685; R2 0.00945 vs 0.00688) and more variants (1270 vs 316), the performance gap is small and both are well below the heritability ceiling, so endpoint alignment is the more reliable tie-break here.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are identical: incident ovarian cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL; same covariates and same validation sample size n=211,958). However, PGS000793 is explicitly derived from PGS000082 but with “inverse variant weights,” which is a strong warning for biological/plausibility and suggests it is not a better-supported PRS construction despite slightly higher full-model AUROC/HR. Since neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 and the small full-model AUROC difference (0.66 vs 0.656) is not a reliable differentiator, the original genome-wide-significant score PGS000082 is better-supported than the inverted-weights derivative PGS000793.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer), have identical variant count (22), ancestry evaluation (EUR), covariates (including family history and smoking/BMI), and essentially identical reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC ~0.745; C-index ~0.742–0.743; HR per SD ~1.49). However, PGS000794 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000083 (“22 variants from Graff et al (PGS000083) with inverse variant weights”), which is a strong negative structural signal because it implies the PRS direction/weights are not the original validated construction. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the safest better-supported record is the original source score PGS000083 rather than an inversely weighted re-expression with no compensating endpoint or PRS-only metric advantage.

PGS000793 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target “ovarian neoplasm”: its phenotyping_reported is a direct incident ovarian cancer endpoint, whereas PGS003394 is explicitly packaged as “10-year ovarian cancer risks,” a horizon-conditioned absolute-risk formulation that is penalized as deployment packaging rather than clean disease-status prediction. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model discrimination difference (0.66 for PGS000793 vs 0.623 for PGS003394) is not a reliable differentiator, especially given PGS000793’s explicitly covariate-heavy model (including family history) and PGS003394’s unknown covariates. With metrics largely non-comparable, PGS000793’s more direct disease endpoint and clearer evaluation context (EUR incident cancer) outweigh PGS003394’s multi-ancestry evaluation and reported training N.

PGS000082 has cleaner endpoint fidelity for the target “ovarian neoplasm”: it is framed as a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”), whereas PGS003394 is explicitly packaged as horizon-conditioned prediction (“10-year ovarian cancer risks”), which domain guidance flags as a negative risk-wrapper signal. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model discrimination difference (0.656 for PGS000082 vs 0.623 C-index for PGS003394) is only weakly informative; however PGS000082 at least provides an HR per SD (1.13) while PGS003394 provides no effect-size evidence. Although PGS003394 is more disease-focused in title and has multi-ancestry evaluation, its unknown covariates plus the 10-year risk packaging make its reported performance less comparable for standalone PRS ranking than PGS000082’s more straightforward incident-cancer endpoint.

PGS002046 is the stronger pick structurally and for likely external transfer: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (570,308) and comes from a portability-focused evaluation across multiple ancestry groups, whereas PGS001255 is a pan-trait UKB sparse framework score ("across 813 traits") with only 213 variants (snpnet), a study archetype that domain guidance flags as often generalizing poorly. Although PGS001255 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6319; PGS-only R2 0.01341) and PGS002046 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial-r=0.0182), both target otosclerosis but PGS001255’s time-to-event phenotyping is a mild endpoint mismatch versus PGS002046’s direct otosclerosis phenotype. Given the tradeoff between clearer metrics (PGS001255) and stronger method/coverage plus less framework-penalized archetype (PGS002046), I select PGS002046, but confidence is low because PGS002046’s comparable PRS-only performance is not directly reported.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well at the surface level (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Osteoporosis). However, PGS001273 provides directly comparable PRS-only performance evidence (PGS-only AUROC=0.5685; PGS-only R2=0.00688) with basic covariates and a clear training/validation context (UKB training n=269,704; EUR validation n=24,905), and its PRS-only R2 is plausibly below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs=0.0036) without obvious inflation signals. In contrast, PGS002768 has stronger structural properties (PRS-CS, genome-wide ~1.09M variants) and a moderate per-SD OR=1.31, but it lacks any PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and has ambiguous endpoint mapping in trait_efo (includes heel bone mineral density), making its support less directly anchored to osteoporosis case-control prediction on the visible fields. Given the benchmark emphasis on endpoint fidelity plus comparable PRS metrics, PGS001273 is better-supported here despite being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite a slight label mismatch (peripheral artery disease vs peripheral vascular disease): its phenotyping is a clear clinical endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”), it comes from a disease-focused PAD study (JAMA Cardiol) with broad multi-cohort development and large multi-ancestry evaluation (n=304,294), and it reports a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.66). In contrast, PGS002055 is an older UKB portability/framework score for an “unspecified” PVD phenotype, with weaker PRS signal evidence (partial-r 0.0175) and much smaller validation (n=19,668), making it less likely to transfer well even though its trait_efo matches the target more exactly.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match to the target trait preeclampsia: its trait_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia” with trait_efo “preeclampsia,” whereas PGS003587 is reported as “Gestational hypertension” (despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported string). Both candidates are near-clones otherwise (same publication, method PRS-CS, similar ~1.09M variants, same training n and EUR-only development/evaluation, same basic covariates, same validation sample size), so the main differentiator is endpoint fidelity plus the available PRS signal proxy: PGS003586 shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.31 vs 1.20 for PGS003587), supporting better discrimination within this sibling pair.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to Parkinson’s disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), come from the same disease-focused Lancet Neurol GWAS meta-analysis, use the same basic covariates (PCs 1–5, age, sex), and have the same validation sample size (n=999), so phenotype and study-context do not differentiate them. With no PRS-only AUC/R² reported for either, the small full-model AUROC difference (0.692 for PGS000903 vs 0.651 for PGS000902) is only weakly informative; however, PGS000903 has materially stronger supporting evidence via a much larger, more polygenic construction (C+T with 1,805 variants vs 90 genome-wide significant variants) and it reports additional effect-size evidence (OR top vs bottom quartile = 6.25; beta reported) that PGS000902 lacks. Given identical endpoint/covariates and same publication family, the richer polygenic model plus stronger ancillary performance/effect-size reporting makes PGS000903 the better-supported choice.

PGS000903 is better supported as a standalone Parkinson disease PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis study family with explicit multi-cohort development (23andMe, IPDGC, UKB, etc.), uses a much richer PRS construction (C+T with 1,805 variants vs 44 GWAS hits in PGS003763), and provides stronger PRS-relevant effect evidence (e.g., OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25) even though only full-model AUROC/R² are shown. PGS003763 is endpoint-aligned but is framed around incident PD in a frailty study, has no training/development details, reports only a modest tertile HR (1.72) without PRS-comparable AUC/R², and looks more like an auxiliary genetic predisposition variable than a primary optimized PD PRS. Both lack PGS-only metrics, so structural/study-design support favors PGS000903.

Both candidates target the same endpoint concept (trait_reported Pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same method/variant count (GWAS-significant, 22 variants) with the same development cohort list, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). Given that, PGS000083 has the stronger available performance signal (higher reported AUROC/C-index ~0.74–0.75 and HR per SD 1.49) and a more general incident pancreatic cancer phenotyping, whereas PGS000663 is horizon-conditioned (0–10 years follow-up) and uses a more clinically augmented covariate set (includes diabetic status and additional collection factors) consistent with risk-package modeling, with lower AUROC (0.67) and slightly weaker effect size (OR 1.44). The large validation N advantage for PGS000083 is only a weak tie-break, but it aligns with the stronger overall evidence package.

PGS004155 has cleaner endpoint fidelity for the generic target trait (phenotyping_reported = "Prostate cancer" with covariates explicitly "0"), whereas PGS005238 is explicitly horizon-packaged (phenotyping_reported = "5-year incident prostate cancer" and covariates = "Age-specific absolute risk adjusted by PGS relative risk"), which is a strong negative signal for standalone PRS comparability and suggests its reported AUROC is dominated by risk-wrapper calibration rather than PRS discrimination. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS005238 (0.789 vs 0.705) is not a reliable differentiator given the heavier/packaged covariate structure. PGS005217 is a disease-focused peripheral artery disease score with a clear clinical endpoint (phenotyping_reported: incident peripheral artery disease) that is a close match to the target peripheral vascular disease spectrum, and it provides supportive PRS signal via a strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.66). Neither reports clean PGS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint/study archetype plus effect-size evidence favors PGS005217.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all psoriasis), come from the same UKB portability publication, use the same training cohort (UKB; n=391,124), have identical covariates, identical ancestry distribution, identical validation sample size (n=19,615), and show essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r 0.0636 for PGS001871 vs 0.0632 for PGS002083; no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either). It also has much larger, clearly described training (UKB n=269,704) and a larger validation sample (n=24,905) with stated multi-ancestry evaluation, even though the selected validation ancestry is European. PGS000342 has slightly cleaner endpoint wording (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported exactly 'Psoriatic arthritis'), but it lacks PRS-only metrics entirely and only provides a low full-model AUROC=0.562 with unknown covariates and no training details, making its predictive support and comparability weaker overall.

PGS004530 is the better-supported choice for pulmonary embolism because it has higher endpoint fidelity (ICD10 I26 in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported) and comes from a disease-focused PRS integration/meta-PRS archetype (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with genome-wide coverage (1,059,939 variants), which domain guidance indicates typically transfers better than pan-trait UKB framework scores. PGS004460 has stronger endpoint fidelity to the target trait via an explicit ICD10 diagnosis definition (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: I26 Pulmonary embolism), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (~1.06M), which is structurally favored for complex polygenic disease risk over sparse pan-trait models. PGS001280, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.60765; R2 0.01403, below the heritability ceiling and thus plausible) and includes multi-ancestry evaluation, comes from a known pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet with only 88 variants) and uses a time-to-event phenotype (TTE PE), both of which are warning signals for external transfer relative to a direct diagnosis endpoint. Given the framework penalty and extreme sparsity of PGS001280, PGS004460 is more likely to generalize better despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2 on the visible record.

PGS005219 is better supported for the target trait (sleep apnea) because it targets the clinically dominant subtype obstructive sleep apnea with explicit matching phenotyping_reported ("Obstructive sleep apnea") and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation. In contrast, PGS003213 is an ExPRSweb framework-derived UKB-only EUR score with weaker apparent predictive signal (full-model AUROC=0.527; OR=1.106) and narrower ancestry evaluation, making it less likely to transfer well despite the broader trait label ("Sleep apnea").

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (squamous cell carcinoma), same method family (GWAS Hits), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same cohorts (MGI) and covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), same training (n=8,029) and validation size (n=8,473), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this, PGS000461 has slightly stronger overall discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.599 vs 0.589; Nagelkerke R² 0.0304 vs 0.0282) and a modestly higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.457), while also using more variants (13 vs 10) within the same GWAS-hits approach. PGS000465’s higher top-1% OR (4.54 vs 3.51) is supportive but not enough to outweigh the broader, more consistent edge for PGS000461 across AUROC/R²/per-SD OR and variant count.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and have identical EUR-only training/evaluation context and sample sizes, so endpoint fidelity and transportability do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on the available full-model/effect-size evidence. PGS000470 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000469: higher AUROC (0.557 vs 0.524), higher pseudo-R² (0.0154 vs 0.00141), stronger per-SD OR (1.308 vs 1.09), and stronger top-1% vs rest OR (2.45 vs 1.48). Although PGS000469 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with many variants (1,119,238 vs 5), within this same-publication sibling comparison the materially stronger observed discrimination/effect sizes favor PGS000470.

PGS005220 is better supported for the target trait (sleep apnea) because its endpoint is a clinically dominant and more specific form (obstructive sleep apnea) with coherent phenotyping_reported = "Obstructive sleep apnea", and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort context (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation noted. Although it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.79) that is not PRS-comparable and includes BMI as a covariate (making the AUROC likely covariate-influenced), it still provides a strong PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD = 1.53). In contrast, PGS003213 is from the ExPRSweb framework (a pan-trait repository archetype) with EUR-only development/evaluation and shows weak discrimination/effect size (AUROC 0.527; OR 1.106), making it less likely to transfer well despite the exact "sleep apnea" label.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused multi-ancestry study, target the same endpoint (thyroid carcinoma; phenotyping_reported matches despite spelling), have identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not decisive). Given this near-clone context, PGS005259 is better supported because it shows materially stronger effect-size evidence (OR=2.04, β=0.71) and slightly higher reported AUROC (0.695 vs 0.686) than PGS005258 (OR=1.02, β=0.016), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (1,085,173 vs 84), which is a positive structural signal when endpoints/covariates are otherwise similar.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication/family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation N (8,473), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (only full-model metrics). Given that, small full-model AUROC/R2 differences are weak but are the only differentiator: PGS000461 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.599 vs 0.593) and Nagelkerke R² (0.0304 vs 0.0268) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.448), while PGS000463 only edges on top-1% OR (3.74 vs 3.51). With endpoints and covariates effectively identical, the modestly stronger overall discrimination/effect-size package favors PGS000461, but the margin is small so confidence is low.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused multi-biobank study, target the same endpoint (trait_efo thyroid carcinoma; phenotyping_reported matches aside from spelling), have the same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.6845 vs 0.6862) is not a meaningful differentiator. The main separable evidence is structural and effect-size support: PGS005260 uses PRS-CS with genome-wide shrinkage and ~1,085,170 variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.96, β≈0.67) than PGS005258’s very weak effect (OR≈1.02, β≈0.016) despite similar full-model AUROC. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the stronger method/variant coverage plus materially stronger effect-size evidence makes PGS005260 better-supported than the sparse P+T 84-variant sibling (PGS005258).

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (T1D), same publication and release date, identical ancestry distribution, identical training cohort (UKB) and training N (804), identical covariates (0), and same validation sample size (n=90,274). With no other differentiators, that modest but consistent edge favors PGS004078 over PGS004035.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study context (same publication), covariates (0), training cohort and size (UKB; n=23,748), evaluation ancestry mix, and validation sample size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and covariates effectively identical, the small but consistent performance edge favors PGS004152: higher full-model AUROC (0.6401 vs 0.6371), higher R² (0.05835 vs 0.05548), and slightly stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.669 vs 1.648; β 0.512 vs 0.499). Additionally, PGS004152 is a MultiPRS ensemble, which is a positive structural signal versus the single-score megaprs.auto in PGS004052. The margin is modest, hence moderate confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same T2D endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication/date, same variant count (800,598), same training cohort and size (UKB; n=23,748), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (n=90,274), and both report only full-model AUROC/R² (no PRS-only metrics) with covariates listed as 0—so performance comparability is essentially identical. With no PRS-only AUC/R² to separate them, the only visible differentiator is the selected European validation record where PGS004068 (megaprs.CV) is marginally higher than PGS004052 (megaprs.auto) on full-model AUROC (0.63771 vs 0.63712), R² (0.05597 vs 0.05548), and OR per SD (1.6509 vs 1.6477). These differences are tiny, hence low confidence, but they consistently favor PGS004068.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all T1D), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), training N (n=804), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). Given that, the differentiators are (i) method structure and (ii) the available full-model/effect-size signals within this same study family: PGS004162 uses an ensemble/multi-score approach (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV), which is structurally favored over a single-score method like LDpred2-auto in this context, and it also shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect sizes in the selected European validation record (AUROC 0.771 vs 0.749; R² 0.141 vs 0.113; OR 2.89 vs 2.67). With no PRS-only metrics available, these within-family advantages support PGS004162 as the better-supported candidate.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and both are UKB-derived framework/portability-style scores with only basic demographic/PC covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). PGS001306 is better supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.630 and PGS-only R2=0.02036 (and these are plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling), whereas PGS001855 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) and no PRS-only AUROC/R2, making cross-model discrimination evidence weaker and less directly benchmark-comparable. Although PGS001855 has more variants (1505 vs 179) and larger training N, the lack of PRS-comparable metrics prevents that structural advantage from outweighing PGS001306’s clearer PRS-only performance evidence.

PGS001250 has clearer PRS-comparable performance evidence for urolithiasis: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.5668) and PGS-only R² (0.00592) in Europeans, whereas PGS001864 provides only a small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0323) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength harder to benchmark. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (PGS001864: “Urinary calculus” mapped to urolithiasis; PGS001250: “Calculus of kidney and ureter” TTE mapped to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis), though PGS001250’s time-to-event phenotyping is a mild mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target. Both are UKB-based framework/portability-style scores with basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation; given similar study archetype, the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics in PGS001250 is the decisive advantage over PGS001864’s weaker/less comparable metric reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all T1D), study context (same publication, UKB development, same ancestry distribution), covariates (0), training size (n=804), and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo and identical phenotyping_reported (“Cancer of bladder”), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (UKB), same training N (12,992), same validation N (13,530), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must lean on within-family empirical performance/effect sizes. PGS000613 is consistently slightly stronger than PGS000611 on the available (full-model) discrimination and PRS association signals: higher AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher OR per SD (1.301 vs 1.284), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.91 vs 2.66). Methodologically, PGS000613 (P+T, 15 variants) is also a marginally richer construction than PGS000611 (GWAS hits, 13 variants). Given the otherwise identical context, these small but consistent advantages favor PGS000613, though the margin is small and based on full-model metrics/effect sizes only.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates. However, PGS001306 is explicitly a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse snpnet model (179 variants) and only modest PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.630, PGS-only R2 0.020), which is a known underperforming archetype for external transfer despite large UKB training/validation. PGS004253 comes from a disease-focused UC study context (immune checkpoint inhibitor–mediated colitis paper) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto; 744,575 variants) with a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.84), supporting meaningful PRS signal even though it lacks explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 (its reported 0.66 AUROC is full-model and not directly comparable). Given the framework penalty and sparsity of PGS001306 versus the disease-focused, genome-wide construction and strong OR for PGS004253, PGS004253 is more likely to generalize better.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation context/validation N (n=19,913). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best differentiators are the PRS-comparable metric available and structural method signals: PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (731,196 vs 5,599), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal when other fields are matched. Hence PGS002075 is better supported than PGS001864 on the visible evidence.

PGS001795 has the cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence for the target umbrella trait: it reports a PRS-only (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R2=0.001948 for uterine cancer in EUR evaluation, which is at least directly attributable to the PRS and can be sanity-checked against the low uterine-cancer heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS003381 provides only full-model AUROC/R2 (AUROC=0.761, R2=0.11) with no PRS-only metric, so its apparently higher AUROC is not comparable and may be largely covariate-driven. Endpoint-wise, PGS003381 targets endometrial carcinoma (a strong match to uterine cancer), but given the lack of PRS-only metrics and its cross-cancer study framing, the more directly quantified PRS signal in PGS001795 outweighs the subtype-vs-umbrella advantage here.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct diagnosis-style phenotype (“Urinary calculus” / “Urinary calculus”) aligned to the umbrella EFO urolithiasis, whereas PGS001250 uses a time-to-event formulation (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. Structurally, PGS002075 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (731,196) versus PGS001250’s very sparse snpnet model (341 variants), a pattern that generally transfers better for complex traits. Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592) and PGS002075 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r 0.0385), that metric advantage is modest and comes from a pan-trait sparse-score framework paper, while PGS002075’s design (genome-wide LDpred2) and phenotype framing are more likely to generalize. Both are UKB-derived with basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decision hinges on endpoint fidelity + method/coverage, favoring PGS002075.

PGS001536 has coherent vitiligo endpoint fields (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both vitiligo time-to-event) and provides clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates and a heritability-sane R2 well below the vitiligo h2_obs ceiling (~0.17). It is also trained at large scale (n=269,704) and evaluated beyond EUR (multi-ancestry eval listed), which supports robustness. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported="Red hair" despite trait_reported="Vitiligo"), lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only a pseudo R2/full_model_r2-like value shown), and has unknown covariates—making its evidence package less reliable for vitiligo PRS selection despite being from a disease-focused paper.

PGS001536 has strong endpoint fidelity to the target trait (phenotyping_reported: "TTE vitiligo"; trait_efo: Vitiligo) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and a large European validation (n=67,425). Its PRS-only R2 is also well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs~0.17), supporting metric plausibility. In contrast, PGS000760 is endpoint-mismatched: phenotyping_reported is "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients" (therapy-induced, different outcome), despite the vitiligo label, and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only an HR=1.41 in a small validation n=1,584). The explicit phenotype mismatch and missing comparable metrics make PGS000760 much less supported for generic vitiligo risk.

PGS001795 is better supported for the target uterine cancer endpoint because it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) and is evaluated at much larger scale (EUR eval n=170,276) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, whereas PGS000541 reports only full-model AUROC (0.576) and pseudo-R2 (0.0133) without PRS-only isolation, making its performance less comparable to standalone PRS quality. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma vs malignant neoplasm of uterus), but structurally PGS001795 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with ~912k variants versus an 18-variant GWAS-hits score in PGS000541, which is more likely to capture polygenic signal. Although PGS001795 comes from a global biobank framework paper (a mild penalty), its stronger PRS-only metric evidence plus much richer evaluation context outweigh PGS000541’s sparse construction and lack of PRS-only performance reporting.

PGS003381 is better supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint is a clinically dominant, high-fidelity subtype match (phenotyping_reported/trait_efo: uterine endometrial carcinoma / endometrial carcinoma), which domain guidance treats as effectively equivalent to uterine carcinoma for most cases. Structurally it is a genome-wide lassosum score with 529,365 variants, which is more likely to capture polygenic signal than PGS000541’s 18-variant GWAS-hits score. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so neither has clean comparable PRS metrics; the higher full-model AUROC for PGS003381 (0.761 vs 0.576) is only weak evidence but is achieved with basic covariates (age + PCs) similar in leakage risk to PGS000541’s basic covariates. PGS000541 has an exact umbrella label (“malignant neoplasm of uterus”) but looks like a repository/framework-style GWAS-hits construction with modest full-model performance and limited polygenic coverage, making it less likely to rank best in external benchmarks.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on study archetype, structural signals, and available PRS-relevant evidence. PGS004253 is a disease-focused UC score (Nat Commun; immune-checkpoint-inhibitor colitis context but UC endpoint) built with a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) and very large variant coverage (744,575), and it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.84), which is meaningful evidence of discriminative signal. PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability framework paper ("Portability of 245 polygenic scores"), uses a very sparse penalized-regression score (1,505 variants) typical of pan-trait frameworks, and its only performance evidence is a modest partial correlation (partial-r 0.0625) without effect-size support. Despite PGS001855 having broader multi-ancestry evaluation and much larger training N, the framework/sparse-model signature plus weaker metric evidence makes it less likely to be the top external performer than the disease-focused, genome-wide LDpred2 score with strong OR evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported and trait_efo align to urinary bladder carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (PGS000723 0.583 vs PGS000613 0.571) is not a reliable differentiator—especially with different covariates. PGS000613 provides more PRS-relevant evidence on the record (per-SD effect size OR=1.301 with CI, plus top-1% vs rest OR=2.91 and pseudo-R²/Brier), and its covariates are basic demographic/PC adjustments (age, sex, batch, PCs), making the reported performance less likely to be distorted by idiosyncratic modeling. In contrast, PGS000723 has sparse reporting beyond full-model AUROC (no effect sizes/other metrics) and uses only 'Genotyping array' as covariate, leaving less interpretable evidence about PRS contribution. Given the richer, cleaner support on-record, PGS000613 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported and trait_efo are identical: bladder cancer / urinary bladder carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is only weak evidence. PGS000723 is better supported by study design/transportability signals: it is developed across many named cohorts (consortium-style) and evaluated in a much larger European sample (n=400,812) with a basic covariate (genotyping array), suggesting broader external robustness. PGS000611 is a UKB-only GWAS-hits score (13 variants) from a repository-style paper with smaller training/validation and its reported metrics include effect sizes but only full-model AUROC with basic covariates; overall it looks more like a single-biobank portability score. Given similar endpoint fidelity and variant counts, the multi-cohort development and large independent evaluation context favor PGS000723.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study context (same publication), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), training N (23,748), and evaluation/ancestry distribution with the same validation size (90,274). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers. On the visible metrics, PGS004152 is consistently slightly stronger than PGS004068 (higher full-model AUROC 0.6401 vs 0.6377; higher R² 0.05835 vs 0.05597; higher OR per SD 1.669 vs 1.651), and it also has a larger variant count (1,071,786 vs 800,598), which is a modest structural advantage. Given otherwise identical design, these small but consistent edges favor PGS004152.

PGS000760 is better supported on PRS-relevant evidence despite both records having major endpoint-fidelity issues. PGS000738 has a severe phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported = "Red hair" rather than vitiligo) and only a small pseudo R² (0.0386) with unclear covariates, making it hard to interpret as vitiligo PRS performance. PGS000760 also has a mismatched, treatment/setting-specific phenotype ("anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients"), but it at least provides a PRS-associated effect size (HR=1.41 per SD, moderate signal) with basic covariate adjustment (5 genotype PCs) and a clearly stated large training context (UKB; n=408,959). With neither candidate offering clean PRS-only AUC/R² and both having phenotype inconsistencies, the moderate HR evidence and cleaner covariate disclosure give PGS000760 a slight edge over PGS000738.
